reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it is presented as a tutorial about deleting a Facebook page or account. The frames show Facebook Pages navigation, page management settings, and the Remove Page section, with no promoted payment flow, promised return, off-platform destination, or request for sensitive viewer information.

citations.quote: Facebook page delete || fb page delete || local tech support
How To Delete Facebook Accont Permanently

opening.argument: The presentation is built around directing viewers to take an immediate account-management action. Its title identifies “local tech support,” while the visual instruction explicitly says “click more” and then points viewers through page controls toward removal. That combination makes this more than a passive discussion: viewers are being guided through a low-barrier action affecting their Facebook asset. The material does not clearly establish who operates the support channel, what safeguards apply, or whether the viewer is being led into a broader interaction beyond the visible screens. The absence of a displayed payment or reward does not by itself establish that the action pathway is benign; it leaves the operational purpose and any associated solicitation unresolved.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense calls this an ordinary tutorial, but its own cited frames show an emphasized “click more” direction and a sequence ending at permanent deletion. Those visuals establish deliberate steering toward a consequential action, not merely general education. The defense also relies on the absence of payment or sensitive-data requests, but that does not establish that no broader solicitation exists outside the sampled screens.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The quoted material shows only navigation to Facebook’s own page settings and deletion screen. “Local tech support” is part of the title, not evidence of a reward, payment request, external claim flow, or deceptive promise. The “click more” overlay identifies a navigation step, while the final screen warns that deletion is permanent; neither quote shows viewers being asked to provide information or transfer anything.

opening.argument: Several presentation choices create a meaningful risk signal when considered together. The video uses large, high-contrast red instructional text saying “click more” and “scroll up,” overlays arrows on the interface, and carries a branded “LTS” mark while presenting itself as “local tech support.” The steps culminate in a screen stating that deleting a page is permanent. This is a highly directive, branded interaction around an irreversible account action. Even without a visible payment demand, the format encourages reliance on the presenter’s instructions while leaving unclear whether the branded source is authorized by Facebook or whether viewers are being funneled to an unshown next step.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense treats missing payment language as dispositive, but risk assessment also concerns how viewers are directed. Here, the branded tutorial uses oversized commands and arrows, then reaches an irreversible deletion confirmation. That combination warrants treating the content as potentially deceptive operational solicitation rather than assuming the unseen context is harmless.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The visual emphasis is ordinary instructional annotation: “click more” and “scroll up” correspond to visible Facebook navigation, and the screen explicitly identifies the operation as permanent. No frame shows an external destination, reward, fee, login request, wallet, or promised outcome. A logo and instructional arrows are not evidence of a scam category without a linked acquisition or payment claim.

opening.argument: Although formatted as instruction, the material also functions as promotion for a branded support identity. The title repeatedly pairs Facebook deletion with “local tech support,” and the frames consistently display an “LTS” mark while directing viewers through the process. The description likewise repeats deletion-related search phrases, including “How To Delete Facebook Accont Permanently” and “how to delete facebook account on Android.” This repeated branding and keyword targeting can steer viewers toward the presenter as the solution for an account problem, rather than simply explaining Facebook’s settings. The video therefore presents a participation pathway centered on the branded source, while withholding clear boundaries about what viewers should do after following the demonstrated steps.
